question: The top of a national exam league table is crowded with small schools. Should a donor pay to create more of them?
options: First check the bottom of the table
answer: Check the bottom first: small schools crowd it too. A year group of 25 swings far more than one of 250, so small schools land at both ends by chance. Howard Wainer showed this after the Gates Foundation had spent heavily on splitting big schools into small ones; it later changed course.
move: Distrust extremes that come from few measurements, in either direction.
ask: Which strong opinion of mine rests on just a handful of experiences?
trap: Yes, small schools do better, as the top of the table shows.

notes: Two equal schools of 25: 84% pass at one, 44% at the other. Top and bottom.
250 pupils each: 61% and 56%. The gap is closing.
2,500 each: 60% and 60%, as built in. Size made the gap, not teaching.

reference: Wainer, The most dangerous equation, American Scientist 95:249–256, 2007
